unit.title: Data
unit.blurb: Tally charts, frequency tables, bar charts, dot plots and pictograms, frequency diagrams for grouped data, and line graphs showing change.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Record, organise, represent and interpret data in tables, bar charts, dot plots and pictograms.

O2.t: Represent and interpret grouped data in frequency diagrams and data that changes over time in line graphs.

p: A **tally chart** records data as you collect it. A **frequency table** shows the totals. A **bar chart** shows each total as a bar.
Always check the **scale**: if it goes up in 2s, a bar between 6 and 8 shows 7.

lesson.t: Why we choose the right chart
p: Different charts show different things: bar charts compare groups, pictograms are quick to read and Venn diagrams show overlap.

lesson.q: Which chart is best to compare the number of pets of each type in a class?

p: Ask what you want to show.
Choose a chart that shows it clearly.
Label the axes and give a title.
Read the label under the bar you need, then read across to the scale.

p: When there are lots of different values, put them into **groups** such as 0–9, 10–19, 20–29. A **frequency diagram** shows how many are in each group.
A **line graph** shows how something changes over time, like temperature through a day. Read across from a point to the scale.
A line graph joins points measured over time, so we can see when a value went up or down and by how much.

lesson.q: A plant was 4 cm on Monday and 10 cm on Friday. How much did it grow?

p: Read the scales on both axes.
Read up from the time and across to the value.
The line between two points gives an estimate of values in between.

options.t: How many are in that group
options.fb: Correct.
It shows the frequency.
The width shows the group; the height shows how many.
